We introduce a novel online algorithm called DART, designed to tackle the non-linear top-K subset identification problem. In this setting, a subset of K items is selected from a pool of N, subject to constraints on the number of items from each category. Our algorithm operates in an online fashion, where unlabelled items are processed one at a time, with the goal of minimizing regret relative to a known optimal subset. DART is based on a variant of the adaptive rejection sampling technique, which has been proven to have sublinear regret under specific conditions on the sampling probabilities. Our results demonstrate that DART is the first non-trivial online algorithm for this problem, with the ability to achieve nearly optimal regret. In addition, we have developed a variant of DART, tailored for the case where sampling probabilities are unknown, which achieves regret bounds that are logarithmic in time. Our work is supported by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, which have been conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our findings suggest that DART is a highly effective solution for the non-linear top-K subset identification problem. The code underlying our work is available online. Abstractive summarization models often struggle to produce high-quality summaries
when dealing with difficult input data, particularly when it lacks essential information.
To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that enhances the model's
performance by incorporating a factual accuracy constraint. This constraint forces
the model to produce summaries that are both coherent and factually correct.
To achieve this, we have developed a new model that integrates a transformer-based
encoder-decoder architecture with a factual accuracy assessment module. This module
utilizes a knowledge graph to evaluate the factual accuracy of the model's generated
summaries. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms
existing models, achieving better performance on fact-checking metrics and summary
coherence. Furthermore, we have found that the model's fact-checking capabilities are
not compromised by its increased focus on coherence. Notably, we have also observed
that the model's performance is not limited to the data used to train the knowledge graph,
but rather, it generalizes well to new and unseen information. Overall, our approach
enables the model to produce accurate summaries without sacrificing coherence. The
source code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishrana/factsum. The results of our experiments are available on the SummEval benchmark.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to examine the competition between alpha-decay and beta-plus decay in the heaviest nuclei, focusing on isotopes with Z=114 to Z=119 and A ranging from 300 to 350. The research employed a microscopic approach to calculate the collective decay widths for both types of decay. The alpha-decay widths were determined using the double folding procedure, while the beta-plus decay widths were calculated using the Gamow shell model. The results showed that the barrier heights for alpha decay decrease as the neutron number increases, leading to a decline in the alpha decay half-lives. Conversely, the beta-plus decay half-lives were found to be largely unaffected by the shell closure, with the primary influence being the beta-plus decay strength. The research revealed that the shell closure at N=82 significantly impacts the beta-plus decay strength, resulting in a substantial increase in the half-lives. The findings indicate that the alpha decay is the primary decay mode for nuclei with N<6, while the beta-plus decay becomes dominant for nuclei with N greater than or equal to 6. The research also suggests that the nuclei with N between 5 and 6 represent a critical region where both decay modes are equally probable. The results were further validated by comparing them with the available experimental data. The 5G and future 6G networks are expected to support a wide range of applications, including those that are critical to public safety and public interest, and are designed to provide high levels of security and reliability. The creation of covert channels in these settings can have severe consequences, and are therefore a pressing issue that needs to be addressed. In this paper, we aim to identify and analyze the risks associated with covert channel exploitation in the downlink of 5G and future 6G networks, and develop a framework to mitigate these threats. The proposed framework involves identifying covert channel transmission methods, detecting covert channel signals, and evaluating the effectiveness of existing techniques in detecting covert channel activity. The results of our analysis highlight the significant risks posed by covert channel exploitation in the downlink of 5G and future 6G networks, and demonstrate the need for further research in this area. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of developing secure and reliable techniques to protect 5G and future 6G networks against covert channel threats. Our findings are supported by simulations of a molecular crystal composed of benzene molecules, which exhibit a phase transition from a low-symmetry to a higher-symmetry state at 6.5 K. Deep learning models are susceptible to adversarial examples that can mislead them. To counter this, adversarial training has been effective in enhancing model robustness. However, the current methods have limitations, as they either focus on specific types of attacks or require extensive computational resources. To overcome these drawbacks, we introduce a novel approach called LADDER, which employs a latent boundary detection module to identify and counter various types of adversaries. LADDER's key features include the use of a latent boundary detector, which assesses the likelihood of test-time adversaries, and an adversary generator, which produces adversarial examples to train the model. Through extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, we demonstrate that LADDER significantly outperforms existing methods in defending against diverse attacks. The code for LADDER will be made publicly available. LADDER's source code can be found at https://github.com/zhongyurcha/LADDER. The associated data can be found at https://drive.google.

Moreover, DPL can be applied to other large-scale models, such as ViLT, to further improve their effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DPL on established zero-shot image classification benchmarks, underscoring its potential as a valuable tool for the computer vision community. To facilitate the evaluation of dehazed images, we have developed a new dataset that includes both subjective and objective evaluations of dehazed images, which can be used to train and test image dehazing algorithms. Deep learning models are vulnerable to sophisticated attacks that manipulate their predictions by introducing stealthy, malicious patterns into the data. In this research, we introduce DeepPayload, a novel black-box attack method that exploits deep learning models by embedding undetectable, malicious patterns into the data. Unlike existing attacks, DeepPayload injects the trigger into the data itself, making it more difficult to identify. Our results show that DeepPayload can successfully compromise a range of black-box models with remarkable accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DeepPayload in real-world scenarios by compromising models used in image classification, object detection, and video segmentation tasks. Notably, DeepPayload can even compromise the most robust models with minimal modifications to the data. Our research highlights the significant vulnerability of deep learning models to sophisticated, malicious patterns and underscores the need for robust defenses against such attacks. The positive-unlabeled learning (PU) scenario is a type of imbalanced learning where the positive class and the positive-unlabeled group exhibit significant imbalance. This imbalance makes it challenging to develop effective models for the positive class. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called self-supervised positive-unlabeled learning (SSPU). This approach involves designing a self-supervised task to enhance the representation of the positive-unlabeled group and leveraging a positive-unlabeled learning algorithm to optimize the positive class. By combining these two components, SSPU can effectively handle the imbalance issue. We provide a theoretical analysis of SSPU's robustness and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on real-world datasets, where SSPU outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both robustness and performance. Additionally, SSPU's efficiency is proven through its superior speed compared to other approaches. The code for SSPU is available at https://github.com/zhongmingwu/SSPU. Our approach, which involves identifying and replacing clusters of data features, can be used in conjunction with various clustering methods and does not require a specific number of data points to function. Through extensive testing, we have found that this method can produce adversarial samples that achieve high success rates while maintaining the original data's appearance. Our method has been successfully applied to multiple datasets and models, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, and has demonstrated its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. We use the geometric Satake equivalence to prove a theorem linking blocks of representations of p-adic unramified groups to certain sheaves on affine flag space components. This has applications in understanding p-adic unramified groups' simple characters and fusion systems based on combinatorial specifications of components in the affine flag variety. As a result, we establish an analogy between p-adic groups near their p-component and non-p-adic groups near their torsion stage. We also provide a geometric interpretation of the Lusztig map and the Springer correspondence in the context of non-p-adic groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the blocks of representations of p-adic unramified groups can be decomposed into direct sums of irreducible representations via sheaf decomposition on the affine flag variety components. This method also allows us to prove a theorem about the decomposition of representations of p-adic unramified groups into direct sums of irreducible representations. We also provide an application of this theorem to the decomposition of representations of p-adic unramified groups into direct sums of simple characters. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the study of finite groups of Lie type and for the Deligne-Lusztig varieties. This paper introduces a novel constraint solver specifically designed for multibody systems that leverages the second-order accurate, unconditionally stable backward dual backward differentiation of time (BDB2) method. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various types of data, including numerical, categorical, and mixed data. The shortest path problem holds immense practical value in diverse fields, 
such as urban planning, traffic management, and supply chain logistics optimization.
The traditional approach to this issue involves the use of Dijkstra's algorithm, 
which although effective, can be computationally expensive and time-consuming.
To address this limitation, researchers have explored alternative methods 
that leverage spatial and graph characteristics to accelerate the process.
In this study, we investigate the potential of deep learning techniques 
to enhance the efficiency of shortest path problem-solving on road networks. 
Our proposed method employs a convolutional neural network to approximate 
the shortest path distance, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through rigorous 
testing on road network datasets, achieving impressive results with a low error 
margin of 2.5% and a correlation coefficient of 0.97. Furthermore, our 
approach exhibits superior performance compared to existing methods, 
demonstrating the potential for significant time savings in real-world applications. 
Our study also highlights the potential for our method to be applied to more 
complex problems, such as the traveling salesman problem, and we provide 
insights into future research directions in this area. 
The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/Arjun-25/SPD-approximation. 
The results of our experiments are presented in the supplementary appendix. 
Our research findings are also showcased through a video available at

By utilizing a highly accurate lightweight DNN model on the edge and a high-performance model in the cloud, AppealNet achieves accurate results while minimizing energy consumption. AppealNet's cloud-based model is designed to be triggered by the edge-based model's confidence intervals, ensuring accurate results while reducing computation costs. AppealNet's architecture is highly scalable, allowing it to handle various types of applications. AppealNet's experiments demonstrate its ability to achieve 96.5% accuracy while reducing energy consumption by 90% compared to traditional cloud-based systems. The evolution of cancer is influenced by multiple factors, including genetic mutations, cell interactions, and interactions between the tumor and the immune system. To better understand the dynamics of cancer, researchers use computational models that can simulate various scenarios and predict the effectiveness of new treatments. However, traditional simulation methods can be time-consuming and resource-intensive, especially when dealing with large, complex models. OG-SPACE uses a probabilistic approach to update cell states, allowing it to run up to 100 times faster than existing methods while maintaining high accuracy. OG-SPACE has been successfully applied to various cancer models, including those of glioblastoma, melanoma, and lung cancer, and has been used to investigate the effects of targeted therapies and the emergence of drug resistance. The relationship between humans and automation is crucial in various fields, such as robotics and self-driving cars, where it directly affects user performance. However, the dynamic nature of this trust has been understudied, with most research focusing on the initial level of trust. In this study, we investigated the impact of real-time interactions between humans and automation on the trust that develops. We found that people's trust is influenced by the performance of the automation in the current task, as well as the level of trust they had previously. Furthermore, we observed that people's trust is affected by the nature of the current interaction, with more significant fluctuations occurring when the automation is under the user's control. These findings highlight the need to consider the dynamic aspects of trust in designing effective automation and to develop strategies to enhance user performance by aligning the automation's actions with the user's goals. Ultimately, this research contributes to our understanding of trust dynamics and suggests avenues for improving the design of automated systems. Current semi-supervised learning (SSL) techniques often rely on a uniform approach, randomly sampling from both labeled and unlabeled data, which can be inefficient. A more effective method is to curate the data, prioritizing those with the greatest potential for learning. To this end, we introduce FlexMatch, a two-stage approach that utilizes a matching process to identify high-value unlabeled data for labeling. The first stage involves a quality assessment of unlabeled data against labeled examples, while the second stage refines this process with iterative improvements. Through this approach, we can create a customized curriculum that optimizes the learning process. Experimental results demonstrate FlexMatch's superior performance over existing SSL methods on image classification tasks. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the effectiveness of each component of FlexMatch. The implementation details can be found at https://github.com/AmnonSofma/FlexMatch. However, the extent to which their ability to understand different languages is utilized in downstream tasks is not well understood. To address this, we developed a novel approach to align text representations across languages. This approach involves first aligning the representations and then using a simple linear classifier to classify them. We tested our approach on various cross-lingual tasks, including sentiment analysis, question-type classification, and named entity recognition. The results indicate that the initial step of alignment is crucial and that ignoring it can negatively impact performance. Moreover, we found that the initial alignment step can be learned from scratch, without pre-training, and that the subsequent classification step can be learned in a few epochs, further highlighting the need to study the initial step of alignment. Overall, our work demonstrates that the initial step of alignment is essential for the cross-lingual capabilities of language models, and that the models can be fine-tuned to perform well on various tasks with minimal training. This study presents a novel controller design for a tethered aerial robot that guides humans by physically interacting with the hand. The objective is to minimize the hand's vibration while navigating the user safely through a desired path. To achieve this, we incorporate a human-state-aware controller that accounts for the user's velocity along the path and steering angle preferences. The controller consists of two components: a path-following controller and a hand vibration reduction controller. Predicting the future trajectory of objects is a fundamental problem in computer vision and robotics. Deep learning models are typically trained on vast amounts of data, but the intricacies of the training process remain opaque. To address this issue, we propose the Deep Learning Task Exchange (DLTE), a comprehensive platform for documenting and disseminating training details of deep learning tasks. The DLTE is designed to facilitate collaboration by providing an accessible, machine-readable framework for training specifications. In this paper, we present the Deep Learning Task Specification (DLSpec), a standardized format for training data that enables automatic execution of tasks. The DLSpec is analogous to a script that guides the training process, incorporating essential details such as dataset, model, and hyperparameters. To ensure its effectiveness, we developed a tool to automatically generate DLSpec files from existing training configurations, making it possible to publish and reproduce deep learning training tasks on the DLTE. The DLTE is expected to promote knowledge sharing, foster collaboration, and accelerate the reproduction and improvement of deep learning techniques. In the context of ALICE, a custom C++ class named UPC was developed to simplify the analysis of charmonium photoproduction. This class streamlines event processing by providing pre-computed values for key quantities, allowing for rapid and detailed explorations of photoproduction dynamics. Building upon UPC is a new C++ framework, named NLO, which incorporates NLO calculations for ${\mathrm J}/\psi$ photoproduction within the kT-Gauss-virtual (kT-GV) framework, and can be easily extended to include other photoproduction processes. NLO is designed to be highly modular and adaptable to different scenarios, making it an ideal tool for in-depth photoproduction analyses. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of both UPC and NLO, highlighting their unique features and applications within ALICE. Additionally, a case study of an in-depth analysis of ${\mathrm J}/\psi$ photoproduction in ultra-peripheral Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV is presented, showcasing the capabilities of these tools. This analysis leverages both UPC and NLO, and focuses on the ${\mathrm J}/\psi$ photoproduction cross section, the nuclear modification factor, and the nuclear scaling parameter. This study demonstrates the potential of UPC and NLO to facilitate detailed photoproduction analyses within ALICE. The code and documentation for UPC and NLO are publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ATLAS-CSC-TP5/photoproduction_analysis. The code and repository will be regularly updated to reflect any changes or improvements made to these tools. The authors welcome contributions from the community and encourage users to submit pull requests with new ideas and features. The code and its repository will be maintained by the ATLAS-Thesis-Photoproduction group, comprising of researchers from the Czech Technical University in Prague, the Institute of Nuclear Physics in Prague, and the University of Geneva. The group is responsible for the code's maintenance and development, and its primary goal is to ensure that it remains up-to-date with the latest developments in photoproduction analyses. The group also aims to provide a platform for users to contribute to the code and ensure its high quality and relevance to photoproduction analyses within ALICE. In this paper, we propose a new framework called distributed reinforcement learning with dataflow fragments (MSRL), which allows for a more flexible and efficient distribution of training tasks.  By breaking down RL training into smaller, independent dataflow fragments, MSRL can be easily distributed across multiple devices, and each fragment can be processed in parallel. Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant breakthroughs in monocular 3D object detection, enabling accurate localization of objects in 3D space using a single 2D image view. However, current methods often rely on depth networks that predict pixel-wise depth maps, necessitating a time-consuming process to transform these maps into point clouds. This paper presents a novel approach, Depth-conditioned Dynamic Message Propagation (DCDMP), which directly incorporates depth information into the message propagation process of voxel-based detectors. By leveraging depth information to dynamically adjust the size of local neighborhoods, DCDMP can effectively capture long-range interactions and reduce computational costs. Our experiments demonstrate that DCDMP achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark, surpassing the previous best result by 0.8 ADE_3D and 0.4 NDS metrics. We introduce a novel, unified policy optimization algorithm, called UPO, designed to address a wide range of continuous control tasks in reinforcement learning. This algorithm effectively handles non-stationary environments and can be applied to various RL problems, including those with changing dynamics, multiple goals, and competitive games. UPO is built upon a general optimization framework that minimizes the expected discrepancy between the model and the actual environment. This framework is combined with a practical, sample-based approach to estimate the discrepancy and a policy update method that leverages the natural policy gradient. The algorithm's versatility is demonstrated through its application to several continuous control tasks, including those with non-stationary dynamics, multiple goals, and competitive games. Experimental results show that UPO achieves state-of-the-art performance in all tested scenarios. The algorithm's code is publicly available at https://github.com/qianhao1995/UPO. Each participant in the system holds a matrix, and our goal is for the system as a whole to calculate a resulting matrix that is the sum of the individual matrices, while adhering to certain linear separability requirements. In the first case, we develop a protocol that is resilient to up to $t$ dishonest participants, and in the second, we show that it is impossible to achieve security without a trusted third party, and in fact, not even with the help of a public-key based cryptographic system. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this method on the BraTS2020 challenge's testing dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. Network diagnosis and troubleshooting rely heavily on the visibility of the data transport path, which is where MPLS comes into play by enabling the discovery of this path through active means. However, MPLS' reliance on the "show" commands for configuration and path validation is limited in its ability to detect any changes to the transport path, including those made by automated systems. This paper introduces TNT, a system that uses the timing of MPLS packets to uncover hidden tunnel configurations, which are not visible through traditional methods. TNT's accuracy in identifying misconfigured tunnels is comparable to existing approaches, offering the additional benefit of detecting previously undetectable issues. Furthermore, TNT's capabilities extend to detecting more complex problems such as looped tunnels and data loss, which are not addressed by existing solutions. TNT's source code is available for review.

Open IE systems have made significant progress in extracting relevant information 
from sentences, but they often struggle to connect this information and provide 
a cohesive understanding of a passage. To address this limitation, we've 
developed Graphene, a novel system that represents passages as interconnected 
clusters of entities and relationships, allowing for a more comprehensive and 
integrated view of the text. By using entity coreference to link these 
clusters and incorporating additional relationship discovery, Graphene is able to 
capture the nuances and context of a passage in a single knowledge graph. Our 
evaluation demonstrates that Graphene is capable of accurately and efficiently 
modeling complex passages, outperforming existing systems in terms of both 
accuracy and scalability. To facilitate further research, we're releasing 
Graphene along with a comprehensive dataset, allowing researchers to build upon 
our work. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/dwadden/graphene.

Our findings also highlight the benefits of neural compression for low-quality video sources, with a 30% reduction in bitrates. A comprehensive cybersecurity system must be able to identify potential threats, execute predefined security protocols, and adapt to changing network conditions. The experiments demonstrate that the reinforcement learning model can effectively identify and respond to threats, resulting in improved security for the control network. By combining the data from these sources, our approach can accurately model human movement and the interaction between individuals and their surroundings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HSC4D through a series of experiments in diverse environments, showcasing its ability to capture complex human-centered scenes. For instance, it can be applied to the development of more immersive virtual reality experiences, the creation of personalized assistive systems, and the design of more efficient robot navigation systems. We anticipate that HSC4D will contribute positively to the advancement of human-centered scene capture technology. The task of salient object detection aims to identify visually striking objects in images.  However, current weakly-supervised methods rely heavily on annotated images, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain.  In response, we propose a novel weakly-supervised approach that leverages a key cognitive principle: humans can quickly identify a limited number of objects within a scene.  By applying this principle to salient object detection, we develop a method that automatically identifies visually salient objects within unlabelled images, using these objects as training data for a subsequent weakly-supervised approach.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, surpassing the performance of current weakly-supervised methods on five benchmark datasets.
